resources.string: How the gut samples its contents

The appendix and ileal Peyer patches are distinct sites of gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT). The sampling close-up follows an ileal patch, and the IgA scene shows a separate part of normal mucosal defense. Sizes and timing are schematic.

The appendix is a narrow, blind-ended tube attached to the cecum. The terminal ileum opens into the cecum separately. Peyer patches lie in the small-intestinal wall and are especially abundant in the distal ileum.

In this appendix cross-section, clusters of lymphoid follicles surround the narrow lumen within the mucosa and submucosa. The separate ileal section shows a Peyer patch: grouped follicles beneath a dome of specialized lining, with villi to either side.
An M cell carries a small sample

In the lining over an ileal follicle, a microfold cell (M cell) can carry a tiny amount of material across the lining to nearby immune cells. The amber speck represents a bit of ordinary food protein.
A T cell checks a displayed fragment

A dendritic cell can display a small fragment of a sampled protein. A nearby T cell can recognize a matching display during contact. Recognizing an ordinary food protein does not mean the gut mounts a defensive response against it.

In a separate area of gut lining, a plasma cell beneath the epithelium releases dimeric IgA (two linked units). Epithelial cells carry it into the lumen using a transport receptor. Secretory IgA helps limit contact between luminal material and the gut lining. This is not an immediate outcome of the sample shown earlier.
